findings.title: Pin and verify the remotely executed installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image build downloads and executes whatever this mutable URL returns as the image build user. A compromised origin, changed script, or substituted response becomes arbitrary code execution in the build and can publish a backdoored image.

findings.title: Fail the build when the installer download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: In Alpine's shell, pipeline status is the status of `sh`; if `curl` fails before producing input, `sh` receives EOF and exits successfully. The Docker build then continues without the intended installation, producing an image with missing dependencies.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: This downloads mutable content from a remote URL and pipes it directly to a root shell during image build. A compromised or changed endpoint can execute arbitrary commands and silently ship a backdoored image.

findings.title: Replace the unverified remote installer
findings.whyItBreaks: The image build executes whatever content the mutable remote URL returns, with the default root user. A changed or compromised endpoint therefore injects arbitrary code into the build and resulting image.

findings.title: Fail the image build when the installer download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: In `/bin/sh`, a pipeline reports the exit status of its final command. If curl fails before producing output, `sh` receives EOF and exits successfully, so Docker can produce an image with the required installation silently skipped.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failure in the public wrapper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported API discards that error and returns "". Callers cannot distinguish a missing key from a present key whose legitimate value is empty, so they may treat failed loads as real data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failure in the exported helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Discarding Load's ErrMissing makes a missing key indistinguishable from a key whose legitimate stored value is "". As an exported API, every caller of LoadOrDefault is forced to treat lookup failure as real data.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key signal
findings.whyItBreaks: When a key is absent, Load returns ErrMissing and an empty string, but this exported API discards ErrMissing. Callers cannot distinguish an absent key from a present key whose legitimate value is "", so they can treat failed loads as real data.

findings.title: Wait for all result sends before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send now runs in an untracked goroutine, so Run returns immediately after scheduling them. A valid caller that closes results after Run returns can cause pending goroutines to panic with "send on closed channel"; callers also cannot rely on all results being available when Run completes.

findings.title: Wait for result senders before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, Run returned only after every `results <- j * 2` completed. The new goroutines continue after Run returns, but Run provides no completion signal. A caller that closes `results` once Run returns can race with these senders and panic with "send on closed channel"; blocked sends can also leak goroutines indefinitely.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, Run returned only after every result had been delivered. It now launches sends and returns immediately. A caller that closes or consumes the results channel after Run returns can miss values or panic when a remaining goroutine sends to the closed channel.

findings.title: Require admin status before granting record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: A session with isAdmin=false and a matching tenantId now receives true, allowing any tenant member to pass the delete authorization check. The prior predicate required both tenant scope and administrator privilege.

findings.title: Restore both delete-authorization requirements
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior policy required an administrator from the record's tenant. The new OR returns true for a non-admin in the same tenant and for an admin from a different tenant, allowing either party to pass a delete authorization check alone.

findings.title: Require administrator status before deleting records
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing && to || makes canDeleteRecord return true for a non-admin whose tenantId matches the record. This regresses the prior authorization boundary and lets any tenant member delete another record in that tenant.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of silently returning defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or incomplete persisted settings are now indistinguishable from valid default settings. updateFontSize then changes the fallback font size and saves it, overwriting the original data; for example, `{ "fontSize": 18 }` previously throws `bad theme`, but now saves `{ "theme": "light", "fontSize": <new size> }`.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures when updating font size
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or schema-invalid saved settings previously threw from parseSettings, preventing updateFontSize from calling save. The new catch converts that failure to defaults; updateFontSize then changes the font size and persists `{ theme: "light", fontSize: size }`, silently discarding the error and overwriting the user's prior theme.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures before saving updated settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or schema-invalid input previously threw through updateFontSize and prevented save(). It now becomes DEFAULTS; updateFontSize then changes fontSize and persists the fallback, silently overwriting the invalid source with a fabricated settings object.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the requested branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", builtFrom is the requested branch commit but artifacts are loaded from the verified commit. The returned report therefore associates the wrong artifacts with its reported source commit.

findings.title: Use the requested branch commit for artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", builtFrom identifies the requested branch commit while artifacts are fetched for the verified commit, producing an internally inconsistent report.

findings.title: Use the requested branch’s commit for artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: For a branch whose ref differs from "verified", the report sets builtFrom to the branch commit but returns artifacts from the verified commit. Consumers therefore receive mislabeled artifact data.

findings.title: Restore the requested entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, the function now returns all reversed entries rather than at most `limit`. In particular, `renderFeed` passes 20 at src/feed.ts:9; inputs with more than 20 entries cause its loop to append past the intended 20-element output.

findings.title: Honor the limit when returning positive-limit entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, recentEntries now returns the entire reversed input instead of at most limit entries. renderFeed passes 20 and iterates every returned entry, so an input with 21 entries produces a result containing 21 entries rather than 20.

findings.title: Restore the limit before returning sorted entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns all entries rather than at most limit. In particular, renderFeed passes 20 at line 9; when all has more than 20 entries, its loop writes beyond the initially allocated 20 slots and returns an oversized feed.

findings.title: Keep the manifest entry count aligned with emitted rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Filtering stale entries removes them from the rendered rows, but the unchanged header still receives entries.length. A manifest with one live and one stale entry declares `# entry-count: 2` while containing one entry, breaking consumers that use the header to validate or preallocate for the manifest contents.

findings.title: Count only emitted entries in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: For entries containing stale records, rows now excludes them while the unchanged header still uses entries.length. A manifest with one live and one stale entry declares `# entry-count: 2` but contains one data row, breaking consumers that use the header as the row count.

findings.title: Count only entries emitted in the manifest
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, the output omits its row but retains entries.length in '# entry-count'. For example, one stale entry produces '# entry-count: 1' with zero data rows, causing consumers that trust the manifest metadata to observe an inconsistent manifest.

findings.title: Preserve the exported shippingQuote API
findings.whyItBreaks: Consumers importing shippingQuote from this module can no longer compile after this change, despite the replacement quoteShipping preserving the same pricing behavior.

findings.title: Retain the shippingQuote export for existing consumers
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was a public export from src/orders.ts and is removed instead of re-exported. Existing consumers importing it from this module will fail to compile or resolve the named export after upgrade.

findings.title: Return the transformed string instead of always throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Every invocation of the public execute(input): string API now throws "always fails"; callers cannot receive the declared string result. The base revision returned input.toUpperCase().

findings.title: Return the transformed input instead of throwing unconditionally
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the public execute(input) function now throws "always fails" rather than returning the uppercase string, so no valid input can complete its intended operation.

findings.title: Restore execution instead of unconditionally throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to execute now throws "always fails", so valid inputs such as "abc" can no longer produce the prior "ABC" result.

findings.title: Preserve eligible viewers on the read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer with fewer than five attempts, this new guard makes isEligible return false. handle then returns "rejected" at line 24, so its existing "read-only" viewer behavior at line 25 is unreachable.

findings.title: Keep active viewers on the read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer below the attempt limit now fails isEligible and handle returns "rejected" at line 24. The existing viewer branch at line 25, which previously returned "read-only", is therefore unreachable.

findings.title: Preserve the active viewer read-only outcome
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer with fewer than five attempts, this guard makes isEligible return false. handle then returns "rejected" at line 24, so its existing viewer-specific "read-only" result at line 25 can no longer be reached.

findings.title: Keep payment gating out of draft saves
findings.whyItBreaks: `saveDraft` shares `canProceed`; an order with `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }` previously returns `"saved"` but now returns `"blocked"`. Payment status may govern submission, but it must not prevent an unpaid draft from being saved.

findings.title: Keep draft saving independent of payment status
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is shared by submitOrder and saveDraft. An order with state "draft" and payment "missing" now fails the new payment predicate, causing saveDraft to return "blocked" instead of "saved".

findings.title: Separate draft saving from the payment gate
findings.whyItBreaks: For an unpaid draft (`{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }`), `canProceed` now returns false and `saveDraft` returns "blocked". Saving a draft is a distinct action from submitting an order and was previously allowed without payment.

findings.title: Read files from the requested channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot reports that channel's commit but lists files from stable. Consumers cannot safely use commit and files as one snapshot, and the prior implementation correctly read both from head.

findings.title: Keep snapshot files tied to the advertised commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from `stable`, the returned Snapshot advertises that channel's head in `commit` and `channel`, but `files` are read from `stable`. Consumers will publish or inspect the wrong revision while believing it belongs to the requested channel.

findings.title: Use the selected channel commit for snapshot files
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot.commit identifies that channel's commit while Snapshot.files is read from stable. Consumers publishing or restoring this snapshot receive content that does not belong to its declared commit.

findings.title: Honor the added limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=1)` still sets `max_count` to 10 and returns ten entries. The added public parameter promises a caller-controlled result limit but has no effect.

findings.title: Honor the limit argument
findings.whyItBreaks: Calling `build("item", limit=1)` still returns 10 entries because the body hard-codes `max_count = 10`. The new public parameter therefore promises a result bound that callers cannot obtain.

findings.title: Honor the limit argument
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=3)` still returns 10 items because the body unconditionally assigns `max_count = 10`; the new parameter's limit contract is therefore false.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public helper promises a positive integer, but `int(value)` accepts `0` and negatives. Callers trusting this contract can produce a zero charge or a negative charge (for example, `charge("-1")` returns `-100`).

findings.title: Enforce positivity promised by parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int('-1') returns -1, despite its new name promising a positive result. charge then produces -100 cents at src/validators.py:7, allowing invalid negative charges through a function callers will reasonably rely on for validation.

findings.title: Enforce the positivity promised by parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public function accepts int("0") and int("-1") without rejection, despite its name promising a positive integer. charge therefore returns 0 or a negative cent amount for inputs that the API now represents as invalid.

findings.title: Preserve the input DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation wrote into df.copy() and left df unchanged. This change writes through df.loc, so callers that retain or reuse their input DataFrame observe its value column unexpectedly modified.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The assignment now targets df directly. Code that retains and reuses the input DataFrame will observe its matching value cells changed after calling apply_values, whereas the previous implementation returned a modified copy and left the input intact.

findings.title: Preserve the caller’s input DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation copied df before applying mappings. This change writes through the caller-provided DataFrame, so aliases to the original unexpectedly observe overwritten value cells.

findings.title: Restore the CI workflow under .github/workflows
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub Actions only discovers workflow YAML files in .github/workflows. Moving this unchanged configuration to docs/ci.md leaves the head revision with no workflow files, so pushes and pull requests no longer run npm ci, lint, or tests despite the README claim.

findings.title: Restore the workflow under .github/workflows
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub Actions only discovers workflow definitions in .github/workflows. This rename removes the repository's sole workflow, so lint and tests no longer run on pushes or pull requests despite README.md:5 promising that they do.

findings.title: Keep CI workflow under .github/workflows
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub only discovers workflow definitions in .github/workflows. Moving this file to docs/ci.md means pushes and pull requests no longer run npm ci, lint, or tests, despite README.md claiming that CI runs on every push.

findings.title: Reject negative values before charging
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public API promises a positive integer, but its unchanged signed parser accepts `"-1"` as `-1`; `charge` then computes `-100` rather than rejecting the non-positive amount.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The public name promises a positive integer, but parsing "-1" returns -1 (and malformed or zero input returns 0). Its in-repo consumer therefore computes charge("-1") as -100, violating the promised contract.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-5")` returns `-5`, contradicting its public name. Its caller `charge` consequently returns `-500`, allowing a negative charge despite relying on a parser whose stated contract is positive input.

findings.title: Borrow items when printing debug output
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` consumes the `Vec<String>`, making the subsequent `items.len()` use a moved value and causing Rust error E0382.

findings.title: Compute paths from the revision emitted in the changeset
findings.whyItBreaks: When `pinnedTag` resolves to revision A and `latest` resolves to B, `changedPaths` are computed against B while `fromRevision` remains A. Consumers replay those paths on A, contrary to the exported Changeset contract, and can apply an incorrect file set.

findings.title: Compute paths from the advertised base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When pinnedTag resolves to a revision different from latest, fromRevision reports the pinned revision but changedPaths are computed from latest. Consumers replaying those paths on fromRevision will omit changes between the pinned revision and latest.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the declared base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: `fromRevision` remains the revision resolved from `pinnedTag`, while `changedPaths` are now computed using the independently resolved `latest` revision. Consumers replay paths on top of `fromRevision` per the exported contract, so a pinned tag that differs from `latest` receives a mismatched changeset and can apply the wrong paths.

findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration renames users.email to users.contact_email, src/query.sql still executes SELECT email FROM users. Applying the upgrade makes that query fail because email no longer exists.

findings.title: Update queries for the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users.email no longer exists, but src/query.sql still executes SELECT email FROM users. Any path using that query fails with an unknown/nonexistent-column SQL error after upgrade.

findings.title: Update queries to use the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users.email no longer exists, but src/query.sql:1 still executes SELECT email FROM users. Any execution after upgrade fails with an unknown-column error.

findings.whyItBreaks: makeClient now ignores each deployment's BILLING_API_KEY and returns one committed bk_live credential. Deployments configured for another billing account will authenticate as the embedded account, and the credential is exposed to every repository reader.

findings.title: Restore environment-sourced billing credentials

findings.title: Restore environment-based billing credential loading
findings.whyItBreaks: The committed bk_live credential is exposed to everyone with repository access and every deployment now uses it, ignoring BILLING_API_KEY. This prevents per-environment credential rotation and requires the exposed credential to be treated as compromised.

findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None for a nonexistent path (lines 6-7); the changed startup path then evaluates settings["workers"], raising TypeError. Before this change, that documented behavior path used one worker.

findings.title: Preserve the fallback for a missing settings file
findings.whyItBreaks: `load_settings()` returns `None` when `path` does not exist, but `startup()` now immediately subscripts that value. A previously supported missing-config startup path therefore raises `TypeError` instead of starting with one worker.

findings.title: Restore handling for absent settings files
findings.whyItBreaks: When the path does not exist, load_settings returns None at line 7. The removed guard previously substituted default settings; startup now evaluates settings["workers"] on None and raises TypeError instead of returning the prior default worker count.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge now logs it and reaches the nil return. Callers cannot distinguish a failed charge from a successful one and may mark an unpaid charge as complete.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge logs it and then returns nil. Callers therefore cannot distinguish a failed charge from a successful one and may record or report payment as completed.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge only logs it and returns nil at line 19. This exported API now makes a declined or failed charge indistinguishable from a successful one.

findings.title: Keep tenant ID in the cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The cache key now depends only on name while fetch still depends on tenantId. After tenant A loads "theme", tenant B requesting "theme" receives tenant A's cached value without calling its store.

findings.title: Preserve the tenant-scoped invalidation API
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported function previously accepted (tenantId, name). Existing TypeScript consumers will fail to compile; JavaScript consumers passing the old two arguments will use tenantId as name and leave the intended setting cached.

findings.title: Keep tenant IDs in settings cache keys
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor now indexes the process-wide cache only by name. After tenant A fetches "theme", tenant B requesting the same name returns tenant A's cached value at line 14 without calling its tenant-scoped store.fetch at line 15.

findings.title: Keep cached settings scoped to their tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: Two tenants requesting the same setting name now share `settings:<name>`. After tenant A populates the cache, tenant B receives tenant A's value without calling `store.fetch`, violating the `tenantId` contract and potentially exposing or applying another tenant's configuration. The changed `invalidate` signature also prevents targeted invalidation of a tenant's setting.

findings.title: Serialize concurrent reservations before persisting
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock=1, two concurrent reserve calls both read remaining=1 before either await completes. Both save 0 and return true, so two reservations succeed for one item.

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock=1, two overlapping reserve calls both read remaining=1 before either awaits save. Both persist 0, both set local stock to 0, and both return true, so one unit is successfully reserved twice.

findings.title: Serialize reservations across the persistence await
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock loaded as 1, two synchronous calls to reserve both read remaining=1 before either await resumes. Both save 0 and both resolve true, so two reservations succeed for one item.

findings.title: Stop multiplying the millisecond backoff in retry
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds, as shown by the paired direct setTimeout use in poll.ts. retry.ts still multiplies its result by 1000, so its first retry waits 1,000,000 ms instead of 1,000 ms; capped retries can wait 30,000,000 ms instead of 30,000 ms.

findings.title: Keep retry's backoff in its original unit
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry() still passes backoff(a) * 1000 to its millisecond-based sleep helper. The first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (16m40s) rather than 1s; later retries can wait up to 30,000,000 ms.

findings.title: Preserve retry's backoff unit after converting the helper to milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry still calls sleep(backoff(a) * 1000). A first failed retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 minutes) instead of 1,000 ms; later retries are likewise inflated until the 30,000,000 ms cap.

findings.title: Propagate output-file close failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is discarded. When Flush succeeds but Close reports a delayed filesystem/writeback error, Save returns nil although the save failed or its durability is unknown. Previously that error was returned.

findings.title: Return errors from closing the output file
findings.whyItBreaks: When Flush succeeds but f.Close fails, the deferred Close error is discarded and Save returns nil. Previously Save returned the Close error, so callers could detect that the write did not complete successfully.

findings.title: Propagate the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is discarded. When Flush succeeds but Close fails, Save now returns nil even though the output was not reliably finalized; before this change it returned that Close error.

findings.title: Include the final item in each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: The half-open bounds return end as the first excluded index, but range(start, end - 1) also excludes end - 1. For rows=["a","b","c"] and page_size=2, page_window returns ["a"] for page 0 and [] for page 1, so render_page and summarize silently omit "b" and "c".

findings.title: Include the final row in each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns an exclusive end index, but range(start, end - 1) stops one position early. Every nonempty page loses its final row; pages of size one are always empty. render_page and summarize consume this truncated window.

findings.title: Include the final row in each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: The bounds helper defines end as exclusive, but range(start, end - 1) excludes both end and end - 1. A two-row page returns only its first row; a one-row final page returns no rows. render_page and summarize therefore silently omit records.

findings.title: Return entries before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: The expiration predicate is inverted: a newly stored entry has age near zero, fails `age > ttlMs`, is deleted, and returns null. Conversely, entries older than the TTL are returned as cache hits.

findings.title: Remove every completed job
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during `forEach` shifts the next job into the current index, then `forEach` advances past it. For example, `[done, done, pending]` returns `[done, pending]`, leaving a completed job queued.

findings.title: Restore the TTL comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: For any non-negative ttlMs, a newly stored entry has age 0 and is deleted as a cache miss, while an entry older than ttlMs is returned indefinitely. This reverses the public TtlCache expiration contract.

findings.title: Filter completed jobs without splicing during iteration
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing while forEach advances its index skips the job shifted into the removed slot. For example, two consecutive done jobs leave the second one in the returned queue, so pruneDone no longer removes all completed jobs.

findings.title: Restore cache hit condition
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has an age below ttlMs, so get() now deletes it and returns null. Once expired, it instead returns the stale value indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice while iterating jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an item shifts the next job into the current index, but forEach advances to the next index. For `[done, done]`, the second completed job remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Return zero for empty input
findings.whyItBreaks: With `rows = []`, `reduce` produces 0 and division by `rows.length` produces `NaN`; previously this public function returned the numeric fallback 0.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller's array
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array.prototype.sort` mutates `rows` in place. Callers that reuse the supplied array now observe it reordered after calling `busiest`, whereas the prior implementation explicitly sorted a copy.

findings.title: Keep empty averages at zero
findings.whyItBreaks: For averageAmount([]), reduce produces 0 and dividing by rows.length produces NaN. The prior public behavior returned 0, so callers can now receive an invalid numeric result for an empty collection.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's row ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows in place. Previously busiest() sorted a defensive copy, so callers could reuse their input order after selecting the busiest row; this change silently reorders that input.

findings.title: Preserve zero result for empty inputs
findings.whyItBreaks: For averageAmount([]), reduce produces 0 and division by rows.length produces 0 / 0, or NaN. The prior public behavior returned 0, so consumers can now propagate NaN into displayed or persisted statistics.

findings.title: Avoid sorting the caller's array
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows. Calling busiest now reorders the caller-owned input array, whereas the previous defensive copy returned the busiest row without changing supplied data.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before reversing
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For scores 9, 100, and 90, rankScores returns [90, 9, 100]; with n=2 the cutoff becomes 9, so topPlayers can retain all players and slice input order, returning a lower-scoring player while excluding a real top player.

findings.title: Restore numeric score ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numeric scores as strings. For players scored 9 and 100 with n=1, the reversed order yields a cutoff of 9; both players pass the filter and slice can return the 9-point player based on input order instead of the 100-point player.

findings.title: Sort scores with a numeric comparator
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator compares score values as strings. For players scored 90, 80, and 100 with n=1, rankScores returns [90, 80, 100], so the cutoff is 90 and topPlayers can return the 90-score player instead of the 100-score player based on input order.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using == can return sooner for signatures that differ earlier, exposing signature-prefix timing information. An attacker can use repeated requests to incrementally forge a valid webhook HMAC and reach processor(payload).

findings.title: Restore constant-time webhook signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: String equality can stop at the first differing character, allowing repeated requests to reveal how much of the secret-derived HMAC matches. An attacker can use response-time differences to incrementally forge a signature and reach processor(payload) through the authentication gate.

findings.title: Restore constant-time webhook signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: String equality may finish sooner for an early mismatch, exposing how much of the expected HMAC matches an attacker-controlled signature. Repeated timing probes can help forge a signature; a successful result reaches handle(), which invokes the webhook processor.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits after the ledger insert at line 23, before either balance update runs. If either update raises, the ledger entry remains committed while one or both account balances were not updated, corrupting transfer state.

findings.title: Keep all transfer writes inside the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the transaction block exits before either balance update runs. If either UPDATE fails, the ledger entry remains; if the second UPDATE fails, the debit can also remain without its matching credit. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance changes in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits after `_record_ledger`, so either balance update can fail after the ledger entry is committed. In particular, a failure of the credit update after the debit succeeds leaves the source account debited, the destination uncredited, and a committed ledger record for an incomplete transfer.

findings.title: Keep billing-day calculation in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation explicitly derived the day in UTC. This now uses the process host timezone: for example, at 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z a host in America/Los_Angeles returns 2025-12-31 instead of 2026-01-01. The same billing event can therefore be assigned to different billing days on differently configured workers.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving billing-day keys
findings.whyItBreaks: For the same instant, this now returns different billing keys on different hosts. For example, in America/Los_Angeles, 2025-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2024-12-31, whereas the prior UTC implementation returned 2025-01-01. This changes exported billingDay and sameBillingDay behavior at day boundaries and can split or misclassify billing records after deployment.

findings.title: Keep billing-day calculation in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: For an instant near midnight UTC, this returns a different day on hosts outside UTC. For example, with TZ=America/Los_Angeles, 2026-01-01T00:30:00.000Z becomes "2025-12-31" rather than the prior stable UTC key "2026-01-01". This makes billing grouping and sameBillingDay results deployment-timezone dependent.

findings.title: Scope memoization keys by tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: After caching account "a" for tenant A, reading account "a" for tenant B uses the same key, returns tenant A's Profile from the cache, and skips fetchProfile for tenant B.

findings.title: Restore tenant to the memoization key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two tenants using the same account value share one memo entry. After tenant A's profile is cached, a read for tenant B returns tenant A's Profile at the cache-hit branch without calling fetchProfile, exposing cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A loads account X, a read for tenant B and account X returns tenant A's cached Profile without calling fetchProfile. Profile explicitly carries its tenant, so the caller receives the wrong tenant's display data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key still throws at line 4, but the new catch converts it to "", which is a legitimate stored value. Direct callers can no longer distinguish a failed lookup from an empty value; loadAll at line 12 now returns an array containing "" where it previously propagated the missing-key error.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key now returns "", which is also a valid value in Map<string, string>. loadAll consequently returns an apparently successful array containing "" instead of propagating the missing-key error, so its callers cannot distinguish absent data from stored empty data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw Error("missing: <key>"); it now returns "", which is also a valid stored value. The exported loadAll caller therefore returns a complete-looking string array with an indistinguishable fabricated value instead of reporting the missing entry.

findings.title: Keep the existing timeout config compatible
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers passing `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` no longer satisfy Config because both `timeout` and `retries` are now required. Existing JavaScript callers compute `Date.now() + undefined`, making the deadline NaN; `Date.now() > deadline` is always false, so retry ignores their timeout.

findings.title: Make retryBackground run outside the caller flow
findings.whyItBreaks: `retryBackground` promises background execution, but it invokes `fn()` directly inside a synchronous loop. A slow callback therefore blocks the caller until it succeeds, fails, or reaches the deadline.

findings.title: Expose exhausted retry failures to callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Every callback exception is discarded, and both retry exhaustion and deadline expiry return the same `void` result as success. Callers of this new exported API cannot distinguish a completed operation from one that never succeeded.

findings.title: Make retryBackground actually run in the background
findings.whyItBreaks: `retryBackground` invokes `fn()` synchronously before returning, so a slow callback blocks its caller exactly like `retry`. The exported name promises observable background execution but the body is a duplicate synchronous retry loop.

findings.title: Surface failure after retryBackground exhausts retries
findings.whyItBreaks: When every callback attempt throws, the catch discards every error and the function returns `void`, indistinguishable from success or deadline expiry. As an exported API, this forces callers to treat failed background work as successful.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config API
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers using the prior `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` Config no longer compile; JavaScript callers instead produce `Date.now() + undefined`, so the deadline guard never expires and all attempts run.

findings.title: Propagate exhausted background failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from `fn` is discarded and the exported function returns `void`, identical to success. Callers cannot distinguish a completed background operation from one whose every attempt failed.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now permits value={42}, but number has no length property. TypeScript rejects this expression; if emitted without type checking, the input renders "len=undefined" for every numeric value.

findings.title: Render the supplied value instead of its length
findings.whyItBreaks: The component previously displayed `value`; it now displays `len=<length>`. Thus `value="abc"` renders `len=3`, while the newly allowed `value={42}` reads a nonexistent `length` property and renders `len=undefined`.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps` now permits a number, but `value.length` is invalid for that union (a TypeScript error). If emitted without type checking, `<Field value={1} />` renders `len=undefined` instead of a meaningful value.

findings.title: Keep the enlarged buffer for git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. The same helper captures the complete PR patch at line 140, so a PR whose unified diff exceeds 1 MiB now terminates git with an output-buffer error and aborts the review instead of posting a result. The prior 64 MiB limit supported these otherwise valid reviews.

findings.title: Restore the buffer for large git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: `patch` is produced by `git diff` at line 140. Removing `maxBuffer` restores Node's 1 MiB default; a larger textual diff makes `spawnSync` fail, and this occurs before the error-handling block, so no review or failure check-run is posted.

findings.title: Preserve a large output buffer for git diff
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses its 1 MiB default. runGithub obtains the full PR patch through this helper, so any diff exceeding that limit produces a non-zero/null status and throws before a review or check run is posted.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox for review runs
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex sends the supplied prompt to Codex with cwd set to opts.repoPath. Removing the prior explicit '-s read-only' means execution can use a write-capable configured/default sandbox, so a prompt or repository instruction can modify the repository being reviewed.

findings.title: Restore the explicit read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous invocation forced Codex into read-only mode. Without -s read-only, the spawned agent inherits its configured sandbox policy; workspace-write or danger-full-access configurations can let a prompt modify opts.repoPath, which is the child process working directory.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox for review runs
findings.whyItBreaks: `codex exec` now uses its configured/default sandbox policy instead of being forced read-only. The default policy permits writes within the working directory, and this function sets that directory to `opts.repoPath`; a review prompt or untrusted repository content can therefore cause changes to the repository being reviewed.

findings.title: Diff the merge base through the requested PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: The adapter accepts PR_HEAD_SHA but now builds both patch and changedFiles from the checkout HEAD. If Actions checks out a merge commit or any SHA other than PR_HEAD_SHA, the review content is for HEAD while postReview/postCheck attach the result to headSha. Also, using PR_BASE_SHA directly instead of its merge base includes base-only changes when the PR branch forked before newer base commits.

findings.title: Compare the requested PR head from its merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: The adapter still identifies the review target as `headSha` (including when `PR_HEAD_SHA` is supplied), but now builds the patch and changed-file set from the checkout's `HEAD`. A PR workflow checked out at a merge ref can therefore review merge-only content while posting against the PR tip. Independently, when the current base SHA has advanced beyond the branch point, diffing `baseSha..headSha` includes base-branch changes absent from the PR branch; the prior merge-base comparison correctly limited the bundle to PR changes.

findings.title: Build the review patch from the configured PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA is H but the Actions checkout is M, this now reviews `baseSha..M` while the bundle and submitted GitHub review target H (lines 165 and 178). The review can therefore describe merge-checkout content rather than the PR commit receiving the result.

findings.title: Retain the merge base when calculating PR changes
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA can be the current target-branch tip rather than the branch point. If the target branch advanced after the PR branch was created, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes target-only commits as deletions, so review() receives unrelated files and a patch that is not the PR's change set. The removed merge-base calculation avoided this.

findings.title: Keep prompt replacement values literal
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets $&, $`, $', and $$ in a string replacement value. JSON.stringify does not escape dollar signs, and bundle.patch is raw source diff content. For example, a patch containing "$&" is inserted as the template match ("{{PATCH}}") rather than the literal source text; $` or $' can inject surrounding prompt text. This corrupts the bundle supplied to the reviewer and/or the patch supplied to the critic, producing reviews from altered input.

findings.title: Preserve literal replacement text
findings.whyItBreaks: String#replace interprets $ tokens in a string replacement. For example, a patch equal to "$&" makes line 33 replace {{PATCH}} with the matched {{PATCH}} token itself, so runCodex at line 34 receives an unresolved placeholder instead of the diff. The same corruption applies to bundle and candidate JSON containing $, silently changing review inputs.

findings.title: Use function replacers for prompt payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets $&, $`, $', and $$ in a string replacement. Bundle JSON, candidate findings, and especially a source patch can legitimately contain these sequences; they will be expanded or altered instead of being passed verbatim to the reviewer/critic, producing a corrupted prompt and potentially an incorrect review result.

findings.title: Keep fallback reviews on the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: If the initial review POST fails and another commit is pushed while the review is running, the fallback now omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit, while the review result was computed from headSha. A REQUEST_CHANGES review can therefore block a newer, unreviewed revision based on stale findings.

findings.title: Keep fallback review pinned to analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the initial review request fails (for example, due to an invalid inline comment), this fallback omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit. If the PR advances after headSha is captured and reviewed, Needlefish can submit a COMMENT or REQUEST_CHANGES result for the old diff against the newer, unreviewed commit.

findings.title: Keep the reviewed commit in the fallback request
findings.whyItBreaks: When the initial review POST fails, this fallback omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit, which can differ from headSha used to generate the diff and verdict if a commit is pushed during review. The bot can therefore approve or request changes against code it never analyzed.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid model/output data such as a finding missing file or lineStart now becomes a purportedly real P1 finding with file "" and lineStart 0. Previously this path raised a validation error, so normalizeReview can no longer distinguish malformed output from a real review finding.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of manufacturing defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid or missing required fields no longer fail validation. For example, an invalid severity is converted to P1 and an invalid category to bug; missing file, line numbers, rationale, and fix become empty or zero values. normalizeReview then returns these as real Finding objects, so callers cannot distinguish invalid review output from a genuine P1 finding.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating reports
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs that previously raised validation errors now become apparently valid findings: an invalid severity becomes P1, an invalid category becomes bug, and missing locations become file="" with line 0. The exported parser gives callers no way to distinguish malformed review output from a genuine finding.

findings.title: Trim category before validating it
findings.whyItBreaks: A raw JSON finding with category "security " was previously normalized to "security"; it now fails the untrimmed membership check and is silently reclassified as "bug".

findings.title: Restore explicit repository targeting for manual ref lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before actions/checkout. Removing -R leaves gh pr view with neither a checked-out repository nor GH_REPO to identify the target repository. The lookup fails or resolves a stale self-hosted workspace remote, and the command substitutions emit empty or wrong head/base outputs consumed by checkout and the review CLI.

findings.title: Keep an explicit repository target for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch intentionally has no pull_request payload, so EVENT_HEAD is empty and it enters this branch. This is the first step, before actions/checkout at line 43, leaving gh pr view with neither --repo nor a checked-out repository from which to infer one. The PR lookup therefore cannot resolve the requested PR and the emitted head/base outputs are empty, preventing the review checkout.

findings.title: Keep an explicit repository when resolving dispatched PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before the checkout at line 43. Without -R (or GH_REPO), gh pr view must infer a local repository, but no repository has been checked out yet. The ref lookup therefore fails or can resolve a stale self-hosted runner workspace, leaving invalid/wrong head and base values for checkout and review.

findings.title: Reject malformed review outputs
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs such as null or {} previously threw a malformed-output error but now become a RawReview with an empty summary and empty arrays. That representation is also valid for a genuine no-findings review, so callers of this exported API cannot distinguish invalid model output from a successful empty review.

findings.title: Reject malformed review payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs such as {} or a payload with summary: 42 now return a RawReview with an empty summary and empty arrays instead of signaling malformed output. The exported API provides no validity indicator, so this is indistinguishable from a legitimate empty review and callers can consume invalid generator/protocol output as real.

findings.title: Reject malformed review output instead of treating it as empty
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed validation errors are replaced with empty strings and arrays. For example, a non-object or an object missing required fields now returns a syntactically valid RawReview with no findings or blocking risks, so callers cannot distinguish an invalid review-provider response from a genuine clean review.

findings.title: Resolve the selected PR's refs for manual runs
findings.whyItBreaks: A `workflow_dispatch` event has no `pull_request` payload. Therefore these expressions fall back to the workflow's dispatched ref and `main`, neither of which is derived from `inputs.pr_number`. Dispatching the workflow from `main` to review a PR targeting a release branch checks out main and fetches main rather than the selected PR head and its actual base branch. The subsequently supplied PR SHA variables are also empty on this event (lines 45-46), replacing the prior `gh pr view` resolution.

findings.title: Resolve PR refs for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, the event has no pull_request object. Both expressions therefore expand to empty strings, despite pr_number being required. The prior Resolve PR refs step queried that PR and supplied its head/base SHAs. Manual reviews now check out github.ref (the workflow-selected ref) and invoke the reviewer without the requested PR revisions, so the manual-review path cannot reliably review the chosen PR.

findings.title: Resolve PR refs for manual workflow runs
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch payloads have no pull_request object, so both expressions evaluate to empty strings. The checkout also falls back to github.ref (the ref selected when dispatching), rather than the PR identified by pr_number. Consequently, a manual run cannot reliably review the requested PR; it receives no base/head SHA overrides and commonly checks out the default branch instead.

findings.title: Restore the Git diff output buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses its 1 MiB default. runLocal obtains the entire patch with `git diff`; a larger diff exceeds that limit, makes the child invocation fail, and line 12 throws before any review is produced.

findings.title: Restore the git diff buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` obtains the complete review payload through `git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"])` at lines 98-100. Removing the prior 64 MiB `maxBuffer` makes `spawnSync` use Node’s 1 MiB default, so a valid diff larger than 1 MiB terminates with a max-buffer error before the review can run.

findings.title: Preserve the git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, Node's spawnSync default is 1 MiB. runLocal reads the complete base..HEAD patch at line 100; any diff exceeding that cap causes spawnSync to terminate with a buffer error, res.status becomes null, and git() throws before a review bundle is created. The previous implementation supported patches up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Mark errored reviews as failures
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub treats a completed neutral check as successful for required status checks. When review(), postReview(), or the success-path postCheck() throws, this catch path now posts Needlefish as neutral even though its own summary says the PR did not pass. A PR requiring the Needlefish check can therefore merge without any completed review.

findings.title: Keep review failures failing
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() throws, this publishes a completed `neutral` Needlefish check. GitHub accepts neutral as successful for required status checks, so a PR can satisfy a required Needlefish check despite no review completing. The process exit code does not protect repositories that require the posted `Needlefish` check itself.

findings.title: Keep review errors as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: A thrown review now posts the Needlefish check with conclusion "neutral" even though the summary says the PR did not pass. GitHub permits neutral required checks, so a required Needlefish check can satisfy merge gating after a review failure. The process exit code only fails the workflow job; it does not change this separately-created check run.

findings.title: Restore a checkout containing the reviewer project
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR-head checkout contains only `.github/workflows/review.yml` and `.needlefish/answers.json`; it has no `package.json`, lockfile, or `src/cli.ts`. `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` therefore has no importer manifest, and the review command's target does not exist. Every review job fails before producing a review.

findings.title: Keep reviewer execution pinned to a trusted revision
findings.whyItBreaks: A same-repository PR can add or modify `src/cli.ts` and its package files; this job checks out that PR head and executes the attacker-controlled CLI with `GH_TOKEN`. The workflow grants that token `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write`, so the PR can forge or alter the review/check results that are meant to evaluate it. The removed trusted checkout was the boundary preventing this.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Restore a runnable reviewer checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR checkout is now the only checkout, but this repository tree contains neither package.json/pnpm-lock.yaml nor src/cli.ts. Consequently pnpm install --frozen-lockfile fails before every review can run.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer checkout trusted
findings.whyItBreaks: This command executes src/cli.ts from the PR head after granting the job a GITHUB_TOKEN with pull-requests: write and checks: write on a self-hosted runner. A same-repository PR can alter that file to forge review/check results or execute arbitrary commands on the runner, defeating the review trust boundary.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The checkout at line 43 resolves to the PR head, so both pnpm install and src/cli.ts now come from the code being reviewed. A PR can add a package lifecycle script or alter the CLI and execute it on the self-hosted runner with GH_TOKEN plus pull-request/check write permissions, allowing it to forge its own review outcome and access runner resources.

findings.title: Install the repository that contains the CLI
findings.whyItBreaks: This repository's HEAD tree contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, or src/cli.ts. The new root-level install therefore has no project manifest, and even if it proceeded the subsequent CLI path does not exist. Future review jobs will fail before producing a review.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Restore canonical severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped raw review data and delegates each finding here. A valid external severity such as " p0 " or "p1" previously normalized to P0/P1; it now fails the exact-match guard and is emitted as P3, silently under-reporting the finding's severity.

findings.title: Normalize severity strings before validating them
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped raw JSON and passes each finding here. Previously, a valid legacy spelling such as " p0 " or "p0" was trimmed and canonicalized to P0; it now fails the exact-match check and becomes P3, indistinguishable from a genuine low-severity finding.

findings.title: Normalize severity strings before assigning the fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped review data and delegates each finding here. A supplied severity such as " p0 " or "p1" was previously canonicalized to P0/P1, but now fails the exact-membership check and is silently emitted as P3, changing the reported severity.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env option, spawnSync inherits process.env. This passes GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN to the Codex process despite the prior explicit credential scrub, exposing CI or developer GitHub credentials to an agent processing repository-controlled content.

findings.title: Restore GitHub-token scrubbing before launching Codex
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an env override, spawnSync inherits process.env, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. runCodex passes its prompt directly to the Codex subprocess and returns its output, so prompt-driven tool/model execution can read and disclose credentials that the prior implementation deliberately withheld.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex child
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env option, spawnSync inherits process.env. GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN are therefore available to the Codex process and to commands it invokes, allowing repository-supplied prompt content to obtain credentials despite read-only filesystem sandboxing.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard for the self-hosted job
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork pull requests now run this job on the self-hosted runner. The job explicitly checks out the fork-controlled SHA, runs its dependency installation, and executes its CLI source, allowing a fork author to execute arbitrary code in the runner environment.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before executing PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork pull requests now reach a self-hosted job that checks out their SHA, runs `pnpm install`, and executes their TypeScript. A fork author can alter dependencies, lifecycle scripts, or the CLI source to execute arbitrary commands on the persistent runner.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard before executing PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork PRs now reach checkout, dependency installation, and the PR-controlled CLI source on a self-hosted runner. A contributor can alter the checked-out code or dependency metadata to execute arbitrary commands in that runner's security context.

findings.title: Continue honoring zero-duration runner settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Both runner duration environment variables previously accepted 0. Now NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 becomes 5000, delaying SIGKILL by five seconds after a timeout; NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 similarly becomes 2000, delaying forced completion. This regresses existing explicit configuration values that request immediate escalation.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner durations
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior parser explicitly accepted 0. Existing users setting NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 to hard-kill immediately after a timeout now receive the 5000 ms fallback instead, delaying termination by five seconds. Likewise, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 now delays completion by 2000 ms.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner timeout overrides
findings.whyItBreaks: A configured value of "0" previously scheduled immediate SIGKILL escalation or immediate post-SIGKILL completion. It now silently becomes the 5000 ms/2000 ms fallback, so existing deployments using NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 wait up to seven extra seconds after a runner timeout.

findings.title: Restore deep coverage for unmapped changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews retain only the six highest-risk mapped hotspots. Files represented only by later hotspots, or omitted by the mapper, are no longer sent to a deep reviewer; the critic receives only the resulting findings plus patch stat, so it can return a verdict without any review of those changed files.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Successful deep reviews can report blocking residual risks, but this path now replaces all of them with an empty array before invoking the critic. The critic therefore cannot distinguish an uncertain deep review from one with no residual risk, and can emit a non-blocking verdict.

findings.title: Keep reviewing after a single deep pass fails
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed or failed Codex response for any one hotspot now rejects reviewLarge and discards results from previously completed hotspots. Previously the failure was recorded as a blocking residual risk and the review continued, allowing callers to receive a usable blocked result.

findings.title: Restore coverage for files outside selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: After selecting at most six hotspots, no changed-file coverage check remains. Any file omitted by the map pass, or assigned only to a hotspot beyond the limit, is never supplied to a deep review.

findings.title: Propagate blockers reported by deep reviewers
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep reviewer can return a blocking residual risk without a finding, but this now replaces all such signals with an empty array before the critic runs. The critic therefore receives the same input for an incomplete review and a fully verified one, and can return an unblocked verdict.

findings.title: Handle a deep-review failure without aborting the review
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed or failed runCodex call for any one hotspot now rejects reviewLarge immediately. Previously it continued reviewing remaining hotspots and returned a blocking residual risk that described the unreviewed scope.

findings.title: Restore coverage for unselected changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews select at most six hotspots, but no longer add a tail hotspot for changed files outside those selections. A bundle with more than ten changed files and seven one-file hotspots deep-reviews only six files; issues in the omitted files can be silently missed and still reach the critic without a coverage risk.

findings.title: Propagate deep-review residual risks
findings.whyItBreaks: A successful deep review can return a blocking residual risk without a finding. This loop now retains only findings and summaries, then supplies an empty residual-risk array to the critic. The critic and final verdict can no longer distinguish an unblocked review from one whose deep pass reported unresolved blocking evidence.

findings.title: Preserve focus in the large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: When a patch exceeds the large-review threshold, review() dispatches to reviewLarge(). This change stops substituting bundle.focus into deep.md and also omits it from the map payload, while reviewSmall() still serializes it. Consequently, a focused large review leaves the deep prompt's {{FOCUS}} placeholder unresolved and cannot constrain hotspot selection or per-hotspot review to the requested area.

findings.title: Preserve focus and deep controls for large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: When a patch exceeds the large-review threshold, review() selects reviewLarge(), but its map bundle now omits both Bundle.focus and Bundle.deep. The deep-review prompt also no longer substitutes focus. Consequently, caller-specified scope/depth controls that are retained by reviewSmall() are ignored for large PRs, producing an unfocused review despite an explicit request.

findings.title: Forward focus and deep controls to the large-review passes
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() selects reviewLarge() for a large patch, both controls are removed from the map prompt; focus is also no longer substituted into each deep-review prompt. The current source has no other focus/deep consumer, so a caller's requested review scope/depth is silently ignored only for large reviews.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For a duration such as 119500ms, minutes is computed as 1 before the remaining seconds round from 59.5 to 60, so rendered stats report "1m 60s" instead of "2m 0s".

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For durations whose remaining seconds round to 60, the formatter emits invalid minute/second normalization: 59,500ms renders as `60s`, and 119,500ms renders as `1m 60s`, whereas the prior implementation rendered `1m 0s` and `2m 0s`. These values are displayed in review timing summaries.

findings.title: Normalize rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 59,500 ms, this computes 0 minutes and 60 seconds, rendering `60s`; for 119,500 ms it renders `1m 60s`. Both differ from the prior normalized output (`1m 0s` and `2m 0s`) used in review timing summaries.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing the guard from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` makes `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` return 0 even though the exported function promises a positive integer and retains an error message stating that requirement. Public callers can now receive an invalid zero value and skip their own positivity validation.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed predicate lets "0" through, and Number("") also becomes 0. The exported function and its error message promise a positive integer, but it now returns 0 to callers.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: `0` is not positive, but `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns `0`. This contradicts both the exported function's `parsePositiveInteger` contract and its unchanged error text, so callers can receive an invalid value while relying on validation.
